stages.title: Consumer behaviour
stages.hook: You have a fixed allowance. Why do you buy the third slice of pizza less happily than the first?
explain: Economists assume consumers try to get the most satisfaction, called utility, from limited money. Each person has a budget constraint: they cannot spend more than they have.

Marginal utility is the extra satisfaction from one more unit. Usually it falls as you consume more of the same thing. This is diminishing marginal utility, and it helps explain why demand curves slope downwards.

A rational consumer compares extra satisfaction per coin across choices. Real people also use habits, are influenced by advertising and friends, and sometimes make mistakes. Economists study both the neat model and these real-world quirks.

example.q: Zara gets 12 units of satisfaction from her first ice cream, 8 from the second and 3 from the third. Each costs 2 coins. If she values a 2-coin notebook at 6 units, what should she buy with 4 coins?
steps: Rank extra satisfaction per 2 coins: ice cream 1 (12), ice cream 2 (8), notebook (6), ice cream 3 (3).
With 4 coins she can pick two of these.
Choose the highest: first and second ice creams (12 + 8 = 20).
example.a: Two ice creams, because their extra satisfaction (12 and 8) beats the notebook (6).

analogies.home: The fifth bowl of rice at dinner brings less joy than the first.
analogies.sport: A fan enjoys the first match of the season more than the tenth.
analogies.music: Hearing a favourite song once is a treat; ten times in a row loses its charm.
analogies.city: The first bus pass saves a lot of effort; a second one adds nothing.

stages.mnemonic: First bite best, last bite less: marginal utility falls.
terms: The satisfaction a person gets from consuming something.
Extra satisfaction from one more unit.
The limit set by how much money you have.
Choosing the option that best meets your goals given your limits.

misc.wrong: Consumers always make perfectly logical choices.
misc.right: The rational model is a useful guide, but real people are also affected by habit, emotion and information.

stages.limits: Utility cannot be measured directly, so it is an idea, not a number you can read off. Behavioural economists study where people systematically depart from the model.

trip.prompt: Find the diamond-water paradox and how marginal utility explains it.

questions.q: Diminishing marginal utility means that...
o: each extra unit gives less additional satisfaction
each extra unit gives more additional satisfaction than the one before
total satisfaction always falls as you consume more
the price of the good falls with each unit bought
questions.why: Extra satisfaction usually declines as you consume more.

questions.q: A budget constraint is...
o: the limit on what you can spend
a kind of tax that is taken off your income
a type of product sold in shops
the price a shop charges for a single good
questions.why: You cannot spend more than your money.

questions.q: Total satisfaction from 1, 2 and 3 slices of cake is 10, 17 and 21 units. What is the marginal utility of the third slice?
Total satisfaction after 2 slices is 17 and after 1 slice is 10. What is the marginal utility of the second slice?
questions.why: 17 − 10 = 7, less than the first slice's 10.

questions.q: Ken likes a drink. After the fourth glass he does not want a fifth. Which idea explains this?
o: Diminishing marginal utility
Inflation, because the price of the drink has gone up
Comparative advantage, because Ken is better at drinking
Fixed cost, since a glass costs the same each time
questions.why: Extra satisfaction fell low enough that more is not worth the price.

questions.q: Why can diminishing marginal utility help explain downward-sloping demand?
o: People will only buy more units if the price falls enough to match lower extra satisfaction
Prices never matter to what buyers choose to purchase
Buyers want to pay more for each later unit than for the first
Supply always rises whenever the number of units bought goes up
questions.why: Because extra units are worth less to buyers, they will pay less for them.

questions.q: Match each concept to its meaning.
pairs: Value of next best option given up
questions.why: Four key ideas in consumer choice.

questions.q: Give one reason real people may not behave exactly like the 'rational consumer' model.
questions.model: People may follow habits, be swayed by advertising or friends, or lack full information or time to compare options.
questions.why: Real choices involve more than a neat calculation.

questions.q: A consumer has 10 coins. A snack gives 5 extra units for 2 coins; a drink gives 6 extra units for 3 coins. Which gives more satisfaction per coin?
o: The snack (2.5 per coin vs 2 per coin)
The drink (2 per coin vs 2.5 per coin for the snack)
They are equal at 2.5 per coin each
Neither gives any satisfaction per coin

questions.q: A friend buys something only because everyone else has it. What does this show?
o: Preferences can be shaped by others
Utility is always fixed and cannot be changed by anyone
Prices do not matter to what people want
He is irrational by definition, whatever his reasons
questions.why: Social influence can shape what people want.

panel.q: Is it sensible to say a person's satisfaction from a bike is '50 units' and another's is '30 units', so the first is happier?
o: No, utility is personal and cannot be compared so simply
Yes, because the units are exact and can be compared directly
Yes, the person with more units is always happier
Utility is measured in coins, so the answer is clear
panel.why: Comparing satisfaction between people is very hard.

panel.q: Why might advertisers care about the idea of marginal utility?
panel.model: Because repeated use of the same product lowers extra satisfaction, advertisers try to offer variety or new features to keep people's demand up.
panel.why: Marketing responds to falling extra satisfaction.

panel.q: Which policy question involves consumer behaviour?
o: Would a sugar tax change what people buy?
How many planets are in the solar system?
What is the speed of light in air?
How tall is the highest mountain in a country?
panel.why: Policies often depend on how consumers respond to prices.

teach.model: Consumers try to get the most satisfaction from their limited money. Each extra unit of the same thing usually gives a bit less satisfaction, called diminishing marginal utility. So people spread their spending across things. For example, the first slice of cake is great but the fourth is not.

points.ask: What happens to the extra enjoyment?

stages.title: Elasticity
stages.hook: If the price of salt doubles you still buy it, but if concert tickets double you may stay home. Why?
explain: Price elasticity of demand (PED) measures how much quantity demanded changes when price changes. PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price, usually quoted as a positive number.

If PED is greater than 1, demand is elastic: buyers are sensitive to price. If it is less than 1, demand is inelastic: buyers are not very sensitive. If it equals 1, it is unit elastic. Goods with close substitutes, or that are luxuries, tend to be more elastic; necessities with few substitutes tend to be less elastic.

Elasticity tells sellers and governments what to expect. If demand is elastic, raising price reduces revenue. If inelastic, raising price raises revenue. Elasticity can differ in the short and long run.

example.q: The price of a snack rises from 10 to 12 coins (+20%). Quantity demanded falls from 100 to 90 (−10%). What is PED, and is demand elastic?
steps: % change in quantity = −10%; % change in price = +20%.
0.5 is less than 1, so demand is inelastic.

analogies.home: Milk for the family is bought almost whatever the price, but fancy snacks are skipped when dear.
analogies.farm: A farmer's rice is a staple with few substitutes; exotic fruit is more price-sensitive.
analogies.sport: If ticket prices double for an ordinary match, many fans stay home.
analogies.city: Bus fare rises hit commuters with no alternative less than those who can walk.

stages.mnemonic: Elastic = stretchy: buyers stretch away when price rises.
terms: % change in quantity demanded divided by % change in price.
PED greater than 1: quantity is sensitive to price.
PED less than 1: quantity is not very sensitive.
A good that can replace another.

misc.wrong: Elasticity is the same as the slope of the demand curve.
misc.right: Elasticity uses percentage changes, so it can differ along a straight demand line even though the slope is constant.

stages.limits: Elasticity estimates depend on time frame, data and method, so economists give ranges. Taxes on inelastic goods raise revenue but may hit poorer households harder.

trip.prompt: Find the table of what makes demand elastic or inelastic.

questions.q: PED is calculated as...
o: % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price
change in price ÷ change in quantity demanded
price × quantity sold
income ÷ price of the good
questions.why: Elasticity compares percentage changes.

questions.q: Price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls 20%. What is PED (as a positive number)?
questions.why: 20 ÷ 10 = 2, so demand is elastic.

questions.q: Price rises 20% and quantity demanded falls 5%. What is PED (positive)?
questions.why: 5 ÷ 20 = 0.25, so demand is inelastic.

questions.q: Demand with PED = 0.4 is...
o: inelastic
elastic
unit elastic
negative supply
questions.why: Less than 1 is inelastic.

questions.q: Which good probably has the most inelastic demand?
o: Insulin for a person with diabetes
A particular brand of crisps in a shop that sells many
Holiday cruises on a ship
A ticket to a concert by a famous band
questions.why: Necessities with no close substitutes are inelastic.

questions.q: A bakery raises its price and revenue falls. What does this suggest about demand?
o: It is elastic
It is inelastic
It is perfectly unit elastic only
PED is negative revenue
questions.why: If quantity falls proportionally more than price rises, revenue falls.

questions.q: A shop sells 200 pens at 5 coins. It raises the price to 6 coins and sells 150. What is the revenue change in coins (new minus old)?
questions.why: Old revenue 1,000; new 6 × 150 = 900; change −100.

questions.q: Match each situation to the likely elasticity.
pairs: Inelastic, as few substitutes and a small share of spending
Elastic, as buyers can easily go without
A brand when many close substitutes exist
Very inelastic, as buyers have no real choice
questions.why: Necessities and goods with few substitutes are less sensitive to price.

questions.q: Explain why more substitutes make demand more elastic.
questions.model: If there are close substitutes, buyers can switch to another product when the price rises, so quantity demanded falls a lot and demand is more elastic.
questions.why: Substitutes give buyers an easy way out.

questions.q: A government taxes cigarettes, which have inelastic demand. What will probably happen to tax revenue?
o: It rises, since consumption falls only a little
It falls to zero, since all buyers stop at once
It cannot change, as the tax is a fixed sum
It always doubles, whatever the tax rate is
questions.why: Inelastic demand means quantity falls less than price rises.

panel.q: A tax on an inelastic necessity raises a lot of money. What is a fair concern?
o: It may hit low-income households hardest
Nobody pays it, since it is taken at the till
It will cut demand to zero within a year
Necessities cost nothing, so no one is affected
panel.why: Policy has revenue and fairness aspects that conflict.

panel.q: Why might demand for petrol be more elastic in the long run than in the short run?
panel.model: Over time people can change their habits, buy more efficient cars or switch to other transport, so they respond more to price than they can in the short run.
panel.why: More options appear as time passes.

panel.q: A seller says 'raising price always raises revenue'. What is the flaw?
o: It is only true if demand is inelastic
It is always true, whatever buyers do
Revenue never changes when the price changes
Price does not affect how much is sold
panel.why: If demand is elastic the lost sales outweigh the higher price.

teach.model: Elasticity shows how much buyers change what they buy when the price changes. If they change a lot, demand is elastic. If they hardly change, it is inelastic. Things with many substitutes, like a brand of snack, are more elastic. Things people need, like medicine, are less elastic.

stages.title: Production costs
stages.hook: A bakery pays the same rent whether it bakes ten loaves or a thousand. What does that do to the cost of each loaf?
explain: Fixed costs do not change with output in the short run, such as rent. Variable costs change with output, such as flour and wages for extra hours. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost.

Average cost is total cost divided by the number of units. Marginal cost is the extra cost of producing one more unit. When fixed costs are spread over more units, average cost tends to fall, which is one reason big producers can have lower costs per unit.
Eventually costs can rise again, for example if a crowded workshop gets inefficient. Firms compare marginal cost with the price to decide how much to produce.

example.q: A workshop has fixed costs of 300 coins. Each chair costs 20 coins in materials and labour. What is the average cost of making 30 chairs?

analogies.farm: A tractor costs the same to own whether it ploughs 5 or 50 hectares; fuel rises with use.
analogies.home: The rent on a kitchen is fixed; the flour is variable.
analogies.city: A bus line's depot cost is fixed; fuel changes with the trips run.
analogies.tech: A software firm pays developers upfront (fixed), and each extra copy costs almost nothing.

stages.mnemonic: Fixed costs sit; variable costs move with the output.
terms: A cost that does not change with output.
A cost that changes with output.
Extra cost of one more unit.

misc.wrong: Making more always lowers cost per unit.
misc.right: Average cost often falls at first, but can rise if the firm grows too large or crowded.

stages.limits: The split between fixed and variable depends on the time period. In the long run all costs can change.

trip.prompt: Look for the shape of the average cost curve and explain why it falls then rises.

questions.q: Which is a fixed cost in the short run?
o: Factory rent
Flour used
Overtime pay
Packaging per item
questions.why: Rent does not depend on output.

questions.q: Fixed costs are 500 coins and variable costs are 700 coins. What is total cost?
Total cost of 40 units is 800 coins. What is the average cost per unit?
Total cost of 10 units is 150 coins and of 11 units is 162 coins. What is the marginal cost of the 11th unit?
Why does average cost often fall as output rises at first?
o: Fixed costs are spread over more units
Variable costs vanish once output passes a certain point
Prices fall for every buyer as the firm grows
Workers work less as more units are made
questions.why: Fixed cost per unit shrinks as output grows.

questions.q: A firm has fixed costs of 1,000 and variable cost of 5 per unit. How many units make average cost 7?
questions.why: Average cost = 1,000 ÷ Q + 5 = 7 gives 1,000 ÷ Q = 2, so Q = 500.

questions.q: Match each cost term to its meaning.
questions.why: Cost vocabulary.

questions.q: Why do large factories often have a lower average cost per unit than small workshops?
questions.model: Fixed costs are shared across many more units, and large firms can use machines, specialised workers and bulk buying, which lowers cost per unit.
questions.why: Economies of scale.

questions.q: A firm's price per unit is 15 and marginal cost of the next unit is 18. What should it do?
o: Not produce that unit, since cost exceeds the price
Produce it anyway, since more output is always good
Raise the cost of the unit to match the price
Ignore the cost and focus on sales alone
questions.why: Producing a unit that costs more than it earns reduces profit.

questions.q: If a cafe is closed for a day, which cost still occurs?
o: Rent
Milk for coffee
Hourly staff wages for that day when they are not scheduled
Electricity for the machines
questions.why: Fixed costs are paid whether or not output occurs.

panel.q: Diseconomies of scale mean average cost...
o: rises when a firm grows too large
always falls as the firm gets larger
never changes however big the firm grows
drops to zero once output is large enough
panel.why: Coordination problems can raise cost per unit in very large firms.

panel.q: A software company has high fixed costs but almost zero cost for each extra copy. Explain what this means for pricing and competition.
panel.model: Average cost per copy falls as more are sold, so big firms can charge low prices and may dominate, which can reduce competition.
panel.why: High fixed and low marginal costs favour large firms.

panel.q: A family sees that making more of its handmade soap lowers average cost. Which issue could stop them from growing forever?
o: Rising marginal costs as space and workers get crowded
Soap becomes free once enough has been made
Fixed costs rise without limit as output grows
Demand always grows with every extra bar made
panel.why: Limits like space and management raise costs.

teach.model: Fixed costs, such as rent, stay the same however much you make. Variable costs, such as flour, grow with output. Average cost is total cost divided by the number of units, and it often falls at first because fixed costs are shared by more units. For example, rent of 300 shared by 30 chairs is 10 per chair.

stages.title: Market competition
stages.hook: If only one shop in town sells bread, how might its prices differ from a town with ten bakeries?
explain: Market structures describe how competitive an industry is. In perfect competition there are many small sellers of identical goods, and none can set the price. In monopoly one firm is the only seller. In oligopoly a few large firms dominate. In monopolistic competition many firms sell similar but differentiated products, like restaurants.

Competition tends to push prices down and quality up, and gives buyers choice. A firm with market power can raise price above cost and restrict output. Governments often have competition rules to limit abuse of power.

Not all large firms are harmful. Some industries, like electricity grids, are natural monopolies because one provider is cheapest, and are often regulated or publicly owned. Economists disagree about how much to intervene.

example.q: In Dorn, one company sells all the electricity. In a different region, 20 farmers sell identical eggs. Which market has more price-setting power per seller?
steps: The electricity company is the only seller: strong market power.
Each egg farmer is one of 20 selling identical eggs; if one charges more, buyers go elsewhere.
So the electricity company has more price-setting power.

analogies.farm: At a big farmers' market many sellers compete; a single remote well sells water to all.
analogies.sport: A league with one dominant club is less competitive than one with many strong teams.
analogies.city: Ten taxis compete on price; one bus line to an island can charge more.
analogies.tech: A few big firms may run most phone apps stores, giving them power.

stages.mnemonic: Many sellers, tame prices; one seller, tall prices.
terms: Many sellers of identical goods; none sets the price.
Something that makes it hard for new firms to join.

misc.wrong: Monopolies always exist because the firm cheats.
misc.right: Some arise from high costs or innovation or are natural monopolies. Problems come from how power is used.

stages.limits: Real markets often sit between the textbook types, and market share alone does not prove harm. Competition authorities judge each case.

trip.prompt: Compare the four types in the table and find an example of each.

questions.q: A monopoly has...
o: one seller
many sellers
no sellers
two buyers only
questions.why: Mono means one.

questions.q: Which is a barrier to entry?
o: A very high start-up cost or a legal licence
Many customers who are keen to buy
Low prices that the firm can set
Plenty of workers who are ready to be hired
questions.why: Barriers keep new firms out.

questions.q: In perfect competition an individual firm...
o: takes the market price as given
sets any price it likes, regardless of rivals
is the only seller in the whole market
pays no costs of any kind
questions.why: Identical goods and many sellers mean no single seller can set price.

questions.q: Three companies sell most of the mobile phone plans in a country. This is closest to...
o: oligopoly
perfect competition
monopoly
barter
questions.why: A few firms dominate.

questions.q: Match each structure to an example.
pairs: The only water supplier in a town
A few big airlines on a route
questions.why: Each fits a pattern of sellers and products.

questions.q: Why might competition benefit buyers?
o: It can push prices down and raise quality
It raises all prices for buyers
It removes choice, so buyers have fewer options
It stops new products from being offered
questions.why: Firms must try to win customers.

questions.q: A town has four bakeries with equal sales. What percentage of the market does each have?
Firm A has 45% of the market, firm B 30%, firm C 15%. What is the combined share of the largest two?
Why are some industries, such as local water pipes, called natural monopolies?
questions.model: It would be very costly and wasteful to build several sets of pipes, so one provider can serve everyone more cheaply, and governments often regulate it.
questions.why: Large fixed costs make one supplier efficient.

questions.q: Two big rivals secretly agree to fix prices. Why do many countries ban this?
o: It harms buyers by removing competition
It lowers prices, which helps buyers
It increases choice, which helps buyers
It helps small shops by making them rivals
questions.why: Price-fixing keeps prices high.

panel.q: A large firm becomes dominant because its product is much better. Should it be broken up?
o: Reasonable people disagree: dominance from quality may help buyers, but power can also be misused
Yes, always, since any large firm is a danger
No, never, since firms can do no harm
Competition has no value for buyers
panel.why: Policy must weigh benefits of innovation against risks of market power.

panel.q: Explain why competition can lead firms to innovate.
panel.model: To win customers from rivals and keep profits, firms try to offer better or cheaper products, which encourages new ideas.
panel.why: Competitive pressure rewards improvement.

panel.q: Why can new online platforms form strong market power even without high factory costs?
o: More users make the platform more valuable to each user
They have no costs of any kind, so rivals cannot compete
They ban all rivals by default from using the web
Users hate choice, so they stay with one platform
panel.why: Network effects favour large platforms.

teach.model: Competition describes how many sellers there are and how much power they have. With many sellers, prices stay low and quality stays high. With one seller, called a monopoly, the firm can charge more. Rules and regulators try to keep competition healthy.

points.ask: What happens when there are many sellers?
What can a monopoly do to prices?

stages.title: Public goods and externalities
stages.hook: A streetlight shines for everyone, even those who did not pay. Why might a private company struggle to provide it?
explain: A public good is non-excludable (you cannot stop people using it) and non-rival (one person's use does not reduce another's). Streetlights, national defence and clean air are examples. Because people can enjoy them without paying, the free rider problem arises, so markets often under-provide them.

An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on people who were not part of a transaction. A factory polluting a river imposes a negative externality; a neighbour planting a beautiful garden gives a positive externality. When externalities exist, the market quantity may be too high (negative) or too low (positive) for society.

Governments can use taxes, subsidies, rules or permits to tackle externalities, and may fund public goods through taxation. Critics note that policies can be costly or mistargeted, and that communities sometimes solve these problems by agreement without government.

example.q: A factory's production costs 50 coins per unit, but its smoke causes 10 coins of health costs for neighbours. What is the full social cost per unit?

analogies.city: A park open to all is a public good; the bus smoke on a street is a negative externality.
analogies.farm: Bees from one farm pollinating the neighbour's crops is a positive externality.
analogies.home: A neighbour's loud music is a negative externality for the street.
analogies.nature: A clean river is enjoyed by all; pollution upstream harms all downstream.

stages.mnemonic: Public goods: Can't exclude, can't use up. Externality: Others bear the cost or get the gift.
terms: A good that is non-excludable and non-rival.
A cost or benefit that affects people outside a transaction.

misc.wrong: Public good means any good provided by the government.
misc.right: Public good is defined by non-excludability and non-rivalry; governments also provide private goods like some schooling.

stages.limits: Few goods are purely public. Many are in between, and some communities manage shared resources well without the state. Estimating external costs in money is hard and contested.

trip.prompt: Find the table that classifies goods by excludability and rivalry.

questions.q: Which best fits a public good?
o: A lighthouse that guides all ships
A pizza that you buy and eat
A pair of shoes that you wear
A ticket to the cinema
questions.why: Everyone nearby benefits and cannot be excluded; use by one ship does not reduce use by another.

questions.q: The free rider problem is that...
o: people can benefit without paying, so too little may be provided
everything is free, so no one needs to pay
buyers pay twice for the same good
public goods cost nothing to make
questions.why: If you can enjoy a good without paying, you have less reason to pay.

questions.q: A negative externality is...
o: a cost imposed on people outside a transaction
a bad tax that is set too high
a loss that a player has in a game
a lower price paid by one buyer
questions.why: Others bear the cost.

questions.q: A neighbour plants flowers that everyone on the street enjoys. This is a...
o: positive externality
negative externality
public cost
tax
questions.why: Others gain without paying.

questions.q: Private cost per unit is 40 coins and external cost per unit is 15 coins. What is the social cost per unit?
Match each example to its type.
pairs: Firm cannot charge people who still use a service
questions.why: Each shows a spillover or sharing problem.

questions.q: If a market ignores a negative externality, the quantity produced is usually...
o: higher than is best for society
lower than is best for society
exactly right for everyone
zero, because nobody wants the good
questions.why: The producer does not pay the full social cost, so it makes too much.

questions.q: Give one policy a government could use to reduce a negative externality such as pollution and one drawback.
questions.model: A tax on pollution makes producers pay for the harm, which cuts output. A drawback is that it can raise prices and it is hard to set at the right level.
questions.why: Policies have benefits and costs.

questions.q: Why do many governments pay for vaccination programmes?
o: Protecting one person also lowers disease risk for others, a positive externality
Vaccines are never costly to make, so firms provide them
Nobody benefits except the person who is vaccinated
Private firms are banned from selling vaccines
questions.why: Social benefits exceed private benefits, so markets alone may under-provide.

questions.q: Which is NOT a public good?
o: A sandwich
Street lighting
Clean air
A weather forecast broadcast to all
questions.why: A sandwich can be withheld and eaten by only one person.

panel.q: Some villages manage shared grazing land without government by agreeing rules. What does this suggest?
o: Collective problems can sometimes be solved by communities, not only by markets or states
Communities never cooperate, so only markets can help
Only a government can ever solve such problems
Grazing land is a public good, so it needs no rules
panel.why: There is evidence for several ways to address shared resources.

panel.q: Why is it hard to set a carbon tax at exactly the right level?
panel.model: The future damage from emissions is uncertain and valued differently by people, so estimating the external cost in money is difficult and contested.
panel.why: External costs are hard to measure.

panel.q: Is it fair that people who do not use a public park still pay taxes that help fund it?
o: Opinions differ: some stress shared benefits, others stress choice, so it is a values question as well
Yes, and no further discussion is needed
No, and no further discussion is needed
Taxes are never used to pay for parks
panel.why: Policy debates mix evidence with values.

teach.model: A public good is something everyone can use and that is not used up by one person, like a streetlight, so people may not pay for it. An externality is a cost or benefit that falls on someone who was not part of the deal, like factory smoke. Governments sometimes tax or subsidise to fix these problems.

points.ask: Why might people not pay for it?

stages.title: Taxation
stages.hook: Roads, schools and clinics need money. Where does it come from, and who should pay how much?
explain: Taxes are payments to the government. Governments use them to fund public services, redistribute income and sometimes to discourage harmful activities. Examples are income tax, sales tax (such as value-added tax, VAT) and taxes on goods like tobacco.

A tax can be proportional (same percentage for everyone), progressive (higher percentage as income rises) or regressive (takes a larger share of low incomes). A sales tax is often regressive because poorer households spend a larger share of income.

Taxes have costs: they can reduce work, saving or buying of the taxed good. Who actually bears a tax, the buyer or seller, depends on elasticity. People disagree about how high taxes should be and who should pay, because these questions involve values about fairness and the role of government.

example.q: In Sorin, income up to 1,000 zeds a month is untaxed and income above that is taxed at 20%. Mei earns 3,000. How much tax does she pay, and what percentage of her income is that?

analogies.city: Everyone contributes a little and the city pays for lighting and clinics.
analogies.sport: Club members pay fees so the club can keep the pitch.
analogies.home: A family puts money into one pot for shared bills.
analogies.farm: A village fund pays for the well and everyone gives a share of the harvest.

stages.mnemonic: Proportional is flat, progressive climbs, regressive hits small incomes harder.
terms: A compulsory payment to the government.
The rate rises as income rises.
Takes a bigger share of low incomes.
A tax on the value added at each stage of sale.

misc.wrong: A higher tax rate always brings in more money.
misc.right: Very high rates can change behaviour and reduce the amount taxed, so the effect on revenue depends on how people respond.

stages.limits: Economists agree on how taxes work but disagree on the best level and design, because people weigh fairness, efficiency and freedom differently.

trip.prompt: Find the difference between direct and indirect taxes.

questions.q: A progressive tax is one where...
o: the rate rises as income rises
everyone pays the same amount
the rate falls as income rises
only firms pay
questions.why: Higher incomes face higher rates.

questions.q: A sales tax of 10% is added to a 80-coin price. How much tax is paid?
Income up to 500 zeds is untaxed. Above that, 30% tax. How much tax on an income of 900?
A flat 10% tax on all spending is called...
o: proportional on spending but may be regressive on income
progressive, since richer people always pay a larger share
a subsidy paid to shoppers
a loan from the government
questions.why: Poorer households spend a larger share of income, so a spending tax takes a bigger share of their income.

questions.q: Match each tax to its type.
pairs: Tax taking larger share from poor
questions.why: Types are classified by how burden changes with income.

questions.q: Why do some governments tax tobacco heavily?
o: To raise revenue and discourage harmful use
To make it cheaper for people to buy
To help the firms advertise their products
Because tobacco is a public good
questions.why: Such taxes have both revenue and health aims.

questions.q: A tax is placed on a good with inelastic demand. Who bears more of the burden?
o: Buyers
Sellers only
Nobody
The government
questions.why: Buyers cannot easily cut back, so more of the tax passes to them.

questions.q: Explain one argument for and one argument against a higher tax on high incomes.
questions.model: For: those with higher incomes can afford to contribute more and it can fund services and reduce inequality. Against: it may reduce incentives to work or invest and some people may avoid it.
questions.why: Both sides reflect real concerns.

questions.q: Tax revenue is 400 million zeds of a 2,000 million zeds economy. What share of the economy is this?
What is a subsidy?
o: A payment from government to lower a cost or encourage an activity
A type of tax that is paid by firms
A loan that a bank gives to a firm
A fine for breaking a rule
questions.why: A subsidy is the opposite direction of a tax.

panel.q: Two politicians disagree about raising income taxes to fund schools. What is the most helpful view?
o: Evidence can show likely effects, but the choice also depends on values about fairness and the role of government
Only one of them can have evidence, so the other should be ignored
Evidence is irrelevant to the choice
Values play no role, since the numbers decide everything
panel.why: Policy debates mix empirical and value questions.

panel.q: Why might a very high tax rate fail to raise as much money as expected?
panel.model: People may work less, avoid or hide income, or move, so the amount that can be taxed shrinks and revenue is lower than the rate suggests.
panel.why: Behaviour responds to rates.

panel.q: A tax cut for a group is described as 'costing' the government money. Why do analysts disagree about its true cost?
o: Behaviour and growth may change, altering revenue
Tax cuts are always free, so they have no cost
Revenue never changes, whatever people do
Costs are fixed by law, so analysts cannot differ
panel.why: Estimates depend on assumptions about how people respond.

teach.model: Taxes are payments to the government that fund public services. A progressive tax takes a larger share from higher incomes, a regressive one takes a larger share from lower incomes. Taxes can change behaviour. For example, a sales tax of 10% on an 80-coin item adds 8 coins.

stages.title: Inflation
stages.hook: A loaf of bread cost 2 coins when your grandparent was young and costs far more now. Does that mean bread got worse?
explain: Inflation is a general rise in prices across the economy over time, so each unit of money buys less. It is usually measured by the percentage change in a price index such as the consumer price index (CPI), which tracks the cost of a typical basket of goods.

Causes include demand growing faster than supply (demand-pull), rising costs of inputs such as energy (cost-push) and expectations of future price rises. Deflation is a general fall in prices. Mild, stable inflation is common; very high inflation can hurt savings and planning.

Inflation affects people differently. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans may gain, savers earning less than inflation lose buying power, and people on fixed incomes can struggle. Real values adjust for inflation, so real wage = money wage adjusted for price changes.

example.q: The CPI is 100 last year and 105 this year. What is the inflation rate? If Ravi's wage stays at 2,000 zeds, did his buying power rise or fall?
steps: Prices rose 5% but his wage did not change.
So his buying power fell, by about 5%.
example.a: 5% inflation, and his buying power fell

analogies.home: A grocery list that cost 100 coins last year costs 105 now.
analogies.farm: If fertiliser and fuel get dearer, farmers raise prices and food costs more.
analogies.city: Rents, bus fares and bread all creeping up together is inflation.
analogies.sport: If every team pays more for the same player, ticket prices go up across the league.

stages.mnemonic: Inflation: money buys less, like a balloon that stretches but holds less value.
terms: A general rise in prices over time.
Consumer price index: tracks the cost of a typical basket.

misc.wrong: If one price rises, that is inflation.
misc.right: Inflation is a general rise across many prices, not a rise in a single item.

stages.limits: CPI is an average, and different households have different baskets. Economists debate causes and the best policy response.

trip.prompt: Find how the consumer price index is built and what the basket contains.

questions.q: Inflation is...
o: a general rise in prices over time
a fall in prices over time
a rise in the price of one good only
a rise in wages and nothing else
questions.why: General and sustained.

questions.q: The CPI rises from 120 to 126. What is the inflation rate in %?
A basket cost 250 coins last year and 260 coins this year. What is the inflation rate in % (nearest 0.1)?
Wages rise 3% while prices rise 5%. What happens to real wages?
o: They fall
They rise
They are unchanged
They double
questions.why: Prices grew faster than wages.

questions.q: A sudden energy price rise pushes up the cost of making many goods. This kind of inflation is called...
o: cost-push
demand-pull
deflation
barter
questions.why: Higher costs push prices up.

questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Index of a typical basket's cost
questions.why: Key words for price changes.

questions.q: Who is most likely hurt by unexpected high inflation?
o: Savers whose interest rate is below inflation
Borrowers who owe money at a fixed rate of interest
People who own goods whose prices are rising
The government, which owes a fixed amount of debt
questions.why: Buying power of savings falls, while debts with fixed payments become easier to repay.

questions.q: A worker earns 1,000 zeds. Prices rise 10%. How many zeds would she need to keep the same buying power?
Explain why very high inflation makes planning for businesses difficult.
questions.model: When prices change quickly and unpredictably, firms cannot be sure of future costs or revenues, so it is hard to set prices, sign long contracts or invest.
questions.why: Uncertainty harms planning.

questions.q: Why does a price index use a basket of many goods?
o: To measure the general price level, not one item
To make the measure more complex than it needs to be
Because the price of a single good never changes
To include only luxury goods in the index
questions.why: Inflation is about the overall level.

panel.q: Economists disagree whether low, steady inflation (around 2%) is a good target. What best describes the debate?
o: Supporters argue it gives room to adjust and avoids deflation; critics note it slowly erodes savings
Everyone agrees, so there is no debate
Nobody studies inflation, so there is no debate
Inflation targets are laws of nature, like gravity
panel.why: There are arguments on both sides.

panel.q: Why can the same inflation rate affect rich and poor households differently?
panel.model: Poorer households spend more of their income on essentials like food and energy, so if those prices rise faster than average, their cost of living rises more than the headline rate.
panel.why: Baskets differ across households.

panel.q: Prices are falling steadily. Why might this worry some economists?
o: People may delay buying, which can reduce demand and jobs
It always helps everyone, so there is no worry
Deflation makes debts smaller, which helps all
Sellers love it because they earn more
panel.why: Falling prices can encourage waiting and raise real debt burdens.

teach.model: Inflation is when prices in general rise over time, so money buys less. It is measured by the percentage change in a price index like the CPI. For example, if the CPI goes from 100 to 105, inflation is 5%. If your pay does not change, you can buy less.

points.ask: Why does it matter to people?

stages.title: Unemployment
stages.hook: Many people are looking for work while employers say they cannot find workers. How can both be true?
explain: The labour force is everyone who is working or actively looking for work. The unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force × 100. People not looking, such as full-time students or retired people, are outside the labour force.

Economists distinguish types. Frictional unemployment is short-term, while people move between jobs. Structural unemployment happens when skills or locations do not match the jobs available, for example after an industry declines. Cyclical unemployment rises in downturns when demand is low. Some unemployment is normal, even in healthy economies.

Unemployment harms income and wellbeing, and also wastes skills. Policies include training, job-matching help, supporting demand, and unemployment benefits. These have trade-offs, such as cost to taxpayers and effects on job search incentives, and economists debate their balance.

example.q: A country has 1,800 people employed and 200 people unemployed and looking for work. What is the unemployment rate?

analogies.farm: After the harvest, seasonal workers may have no work until planting.
analogies.city: A factory closing leaves workers with skills the other employers do not need.
analogies.sport: A player between clubs is briefly out of work: frictional.
analogies.tech: New software replaces a task and workers must retrain.

stages.mnemonic: Frictional is between jobs, structural is mismatched skills, cyclical follows the boom and bust.
terms: People who are employed or actively seeking work.
Unemployed as a percentage of the labour force.
Caused by a mismatch of skills or place.
Caused by low demand in a downturn.

misc.wrong: Everyone without a job is counted as unemployed.
misc.right: Only people actively looking for work count; students, retirees and those not looking are outside the labour force.

stages.limits: Official rates can hide people who gave up looking or work fewer hours than they want. Definitions vary across countries.

trip.prompt: Find the types of unemployment and an example of each.

questions.q: The labour force includes...
o: employed people and those actively seeking work
everyone who lives in the country
only people who have a job
only students in full-time education
questions.why: Both employed and job-seeking unemployed count.

questions.q: A town has 4,500 employed and 500 unemployed people. What is the unemployment rate in %?
The labour force is 20,000 and the unemployment rate is 6%. How many people are unemployed?
A tailor loses her job when a clothes factory closes and her skills do not match local vacancies. This is...
o: structural unemployment
frictional unemployment
cyclical unemployment
not unemployment
questions.why: Skills mismatch with available jobs.

questions.q: A graduate searches for two months before a good job. This is mostly...
o: frictional unemployment
structural unemployment
cyclical unemployment
deflation
questions.why: Short-term movement between jobs or into the labour market.

questions.q: Match each type to a cause.
pairs: Work depends on the time of year
questions.why: Different causes need different policies.

questions.q: A full-time student who is not looking for work is counted as...
o: outside the labour force
unemployed, since they have no job
employed, since studying is work
retired from work
questions.why: Not working and not seeking work.

questions.q: Suggest one policy to reduce structural unemployment and one possible drawback.
questions.model: Retraining programmes can help workers gain the skills employers want, but they cost money and take time, and may not match future jobs.
questions.why: Policies have costs and limits.

questions.q: Why would a government worry more about cyclical than frictional unemployment?
o: It reflects weak demand and idle capacity, not normal job moves
Frictional is bigger and so is the only problem
Cyclical is voluntary, so it is no worry
It is the same as frictional in every way
questions.why: Cyclical unemployment signals the economy running below its potential.

questions.q: If many discouraged workers stop looking for jobs, what happens to the measured unemployment rate?
o: It may fall even though they have no jobs
It must rise, since fewer people have jobs
It is unchanged, since they are still counted
It becomes negative
questions.why: They leave the labour force, so the rate can understate hidden joblessness.

panel.q: Unemployment benefits help families but critics say they can lengthen job searches. What is the best view?
o: Both effects can exist, so designing benefits involves trade-offs
Benefits always cause unemployment, so they should end
Benefits never matter to how long people search
Search is unaffected by benefits in any way
panel.why: Benefits cushion hardship and can affect incentives; evidence is debated.

panel.q: Why might new technology reduce some jobs yet create others?
panel.model: Technology can replace some tasks, but it also creates new products, industries and roles. Workers may face a difficult transition if their skills do not match the new jobs.
panel.why: Technology changes job composition.

panel.q: Is zero unemployment a realistic goal?
o: Unlikely, since some people are always changing jobs or industries
Yes, easily, since everyone can have a job at once
No, because the labour force is zero
It is illegal to aim for it
panel.why: Frictional unemployment exists even in strong economies.

teach.model: A person is unemployed if they have no job but are actively looking. The unemployment rate is the unemployed divided by the labour force. There are different kinds: moving between jobs, mismatched skills and weak demand. For example, 200 unemployed out of a labour force of 2,000 is 10%.

points.ask: How do you work out the rate?

stages.title: Economic growth
stages.hook: One country's economy grows 3% every year and another's grows 1%. After many years, how different will they be?
explain: Economic growth is an increase in the amount of goods and services an economy produces, usually measured by the percentage change in real GDP (gross domestic product adjusted for inflation). GDP per person is often used to compare living standards.

Growth comes from more inputs (more workers, more capital, more resources) and from higher productivity: better technology, skills and organisation. Growth compounds, so small differences in growth rates add up to large gaps over decades. A handy rule: years to double ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate in %.

GDP growth does not measure everything. It misses unpaid work, inequality, and environmental damage, so people also look at health, education and other measures. Many people debate how to balance growth with the environment and fairness.

example.q: The economy of Veldra has real GDP of 500 billion zeds. It grows 4% in a year. What is the new GDP, and about how many years to double at 4% a year?
steps: This is a rule of thumb, not exact.
example.a: 520 billion zeds; about 17.5 years to double

analogies.farm: A bigger harvest from better seeds and tools is growth.
analogies.city: A city that adds new factories and trains workers can produce more.
analogies.nature: A tree grows slowly at first and then adds more each year as it gets bigger, like compounding.
analogies.tech: A new machine lets one worker produce more, raising productivity.

stages.mnemonic: Rule of 70: divide 70 by the growth rate to find the doubling time.
terms: The value of final goods and services produced in a country in a period.
Output per worker or per hour.
Rise in real GDP over time.

misc.wrong: A rising GDP means everyone is better off.
misc.right: GDP is an average total; the gains may be shared unequally, and GDP ignores things like pollution and unpaid work.

stages.limits: GDP is a useful but imperfect measure, and economists disagree whether and how growth should be limited for environmental reasons.

trip.prompt: Find the main sources of growth and how it is measured.

questions.q: Real GDP is...
o: GDP adjusted for inflation
GDP counted twice to be safe
GDP that leaves out all services
GDP per hour that people work
questions.why: Removing price changes shows actual output change.

questions.q: GDP rises from 200 to 210 billion zeds (real). What is the growth rate in %?
An economy of 1,000 billion zeds grows by 3% in each of two years. What is its size after two years, to the nearest billion?
Using the rule of 70, about how many years will it take an economy growing at 2% a year to double?
GDP is 600 billion zeds and the population is 20 million. What is GDP per person?
o: 30,000 zeds
3,000 zeds
12 zeds
questions.why: 600 billion ÷ 20 million = 30,000 zeds per person.

questions.q: Productivity is...
o: output per worker or per hour
the total number of workers in a country
the price of goods in the shops
the rate of interest on loans
questions.why: It measures how efficiently inputs are used.

questions.q: Match each source of growth.
questions.why: Growth comes from inputs and productivity.

questions.q: Why does a small difference in growth rates matter a lot over decades?
o: Growth compounds
Growth adds a fixed amount
Rates cancel out
Population disappears
questions.why: Each year's growth builds on a bigger base.

questions.q: Name two things that GDP does not measure well, and say why that matters.
questions.model: GDP misses unpaid work such as home care, environmental damage and how income is shared, so a rising GDP does not mean everyone's quality of life is improving.
questions.why: GDP is incomplete as a welfare measure.

questions.q: GDP grows 4% while the population grows 4%. What happens to GDP per person?
o: It stays about the same
It doubles, since both numbers have grown
It falls to zero
It rises by 8%
questions.why: Output per person is unchanged if both rise equally.

panel.q: Some argue that rich countries should aim for less growth to protect nature; others argue growth helps fund solutions. What is a fair summary?
o: It is a contested question that involves evidence and values
One side is simply wrong, whatever evidence is shown
Growth has no effect on nature
Nature has no value in economics
panel.why: Economists and others disagree about the trade-offs.

panel.q: Why do economists focus on productivity growth rather than just adding more workers?
panel.model: Adding workers raises total output but not output per person, and the number of workers is limited. Higher productivity raises output per worker, which is what lifts living standards over time.
panel.why: Productivity drives income per person.

panel.q: A country's GDP grows fast but most gains go to a small group. How should this be judged?
o: Growth is useful but how it is shared also matters, and people weigh fairness differently
Growth is all that matters, however it is shared
Distribution is irrelevant to how well people live
Nothing can be said about it
panel.why: Both the size and the sharing of output matter.

teach.model: Economic growth means an economy produces more goods and services over time, measured by the rise in real GDP. It comes from more workers and machines and especially from higher productivity. Growth compounds, so small differences build up. For example, 3% a year doubles an economy in about 23 years.
